
## Theory Questions
A sinusoidal voltage source with a 50 Ohm output impedance is used to drive a Helmholtz coil with 75 turns and a radius of 1cm. What is the coil magnetic flux density, B, as a function of voltage amplitude, Vzp, and frequency, f?  

In a Helmholtz coil,

$$
\begin{align}
B(x) = \frac{\mu_{0}nI R^{2}}{2} \left[ \left( \frac{1}{R^{2} + \left( x-\frac{R}{2} \right)^{2}} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} +   \left( \frac{1}{R^{2} + \left( x+\frac{R}{2} \right)^{2}} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \right]
\end{align}
$$
According to sciencefacts.net, this simplifies to:
$$
\begin{align}
B = \left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \frac{\mu_{0}NI}{R}
\end{align}
$$

where $x$ is the position along the central axis of the coil. 


We can say that the voltage is
$$
\begin{align}
V(t) = \sin\left( 2\pi f t \right)
\end{align}
$$

This gives a current from the source (not including the inductive behavior)
$$
\begin{align}
I(t) = \frac{V(t)}{50\Omega} = \frac{\sin\left( 2\pi ft \right)}{50}
\end{align}
$$

We can find the frequency dependent impedance, which corresponds to a voltage drop, which we would subtract away from the $V_{zp}\sin(2\pi ft)$ term.

$Z=j\omega L$
And thus a total current
$$
\begin{align}
I_{tot}  =  \frac{V_{zp} \sin(2\pi ft)}{50+j\omega L}  
\end{align}
$$
We have one more step. Recall that
$$
\begin{align}
B  & =  \left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \frac{\mu_{0}NI}{R} \\
\end{align}
$$
The inductance $L$ is flux per current.
$$
\begin{align}
L &  = \frac{\pi R^{2}B}{I} \\
L  & = \mu_{0}N\pi R \left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \\
 & = 2.12 \mu H
\end{align}
$$
This finally gives us
$$
\begin{align}
 B & = \left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \frac{\mu_{0}N V_{zp} \sin(2\pi ft) }{(50+j\omega L)R} \\ 
 B & = \left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \frac{\mu_{0}N V_{zp} \sin(2\pi ft) }{\left( 50+j\omega \left( \mu_{0}N\pi R \left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \right) \right)R}
\end{align}
$$

We are given $\mu_{0}$, $N$, $\omega=2\pi f$, and $R$. Therefore, we have a function in terms of $V_{zp}$, $f$, $t$.




Because the magnetic field is constant inside of the Helmholtz coil, the flux is just $B*2\pi R$ and the flux density is  $\frac{B*2\pi R}{2\pi R}= B$. 


# old work

$V_{\text{ counter emf }} = - \frac{ d I}{d t }= -\frac{2\pi f\cos(2\pi ft)}{50+j\omega L}$
This gives us a total voltage
$$
\begin{align}
V_{tot}  = V_{zp}  \left( \sin(2\pi ft)-\frac{2\pi ft}{50+j\omega L}\cos(2\pi ft) \right)  \\
I_{tot}  =  \frac{V_{zp}}{50}  \left( \sin(2\pi ft)-\frac{2\pi ft}{50+j\omega L}\cos(2\pi ft) \right) 
\end{align}
$$



$$
\begin{align}
B  & =  \left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \frac{\mu_{0}NI}{R} \\
 & = \left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \frac{\mu_{0}N V_{zp} \sin(2\pi ft)}{50R}
\end{align}
$$






2. What is the magnetic field at radius R away from an infinitely long wire carrying current I? You can derive this from Maxwell by finding the integral form of the equations and taking a path integral, or you can just look it up.


I just realized we can just look it up. :( I've done this homework problem before and it is moderately satisfying. Starting from 

$$
\begin{align}
\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_{0}I_{_{enc} } + 0 
\end{align}
$$
we make a gaussian cylinder, use symmetry to cancel non perpendicular components, and have a nasty integral that evaluates to just 1. 
$$
\boxed{
B = \frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi R}
}
$$

14. Put your probe in the Helmholtz coil, turn on your signal generator and do some basic checks: do you see a B field response at the frequency you are driving in? Does the B field response go away when you take your probe out of the Helmholtz coil? Does the power of the response change when you change the power of your input? Does the frequency of your response change when you change the frequency of your input?
    

We see frequency dependence, and that the $\vec{B}$ field depends on the position of the probe. As i decrease the power we dump into the coil from 20 $dbm$ to $0$ and below, we see the reading go down and hit the noise floor. Electricity works like we think it should.

19. Measure field around an “infinite” wire
    
We put a wire in a breadboard across the length, with a 100 ohm resistor
close to the wire we see about -57 dBm

With our arm about 37 cm (way more precision than we actually have - we said my shoe was a foot and guessed 2 inches above that) above the board, we measured -67 dBm. 
  
We didn't use this helmholtz coil. We used the big beefy one. We didn't look down here for photos, and saw it too late.

We see that 1cm away, we expect to see 500 nT, and we read off of the probe 700 nT. Thats pretty close (ish).

At 37 cm away, we see dramatically different numbers - probably from stray magnetic fields and insensitivity or something. Theoretically 13 nT, but experimentally 348 nT. Ouchies.
